questions.question:
**Select the option that will improve the underlined part of the given sentence. In case no improvement is needed, select 'No improvement required'.**

The farmer was __deprived from__ his land by the money lender.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is option 2), i.e., 'deprived of.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__** 

__
 
• The error lies in Part (deprived from) of the sentence.
 
• As per instructions, the remaining portion of the sentence is correct.
 
• According to the rules of prepositions, **'from'** is used to show the place where someone or something starts; used to show the material of which something is made; to show a change in the state of someone or something.
 
• The preposition **'of' **is used to indicate relating to, belonging to; to indicate reference, or to specify the number or an amount.
 
• Deprive forms the phrasal verb **'deprive of' **which means to take something away from someone, especially something valuable or pleasurable.
 
• Therefore, in the erroneous part, the use of the preposition 'from' in the sentence should be replaced with the preposition 'of' to make it grammatically correct.
 
• Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Correct sentence:__ *The farmer was** __deprived of__ **his land by the money lender. *

• In the Indirect speech **'said'** will be changed into **'hoped.'**
 
• The indirect speech will begin like **'The traveller hoped that.'**
 
• Now we have to change the reported speech.
 
• Here** 'I' **will be changed into **'he.'**
 
• **'My' **will be changed to** 'his'.**
 
• Here, the future indefinite tense** 'won't'** will be changed into the past indefinite tense** 'wouldn't.'**

• While changing the voice of an **imperative sentence**, follow the steps given below:

• **You are ordered/requested/advised etc. + to + V1 + object **
 
• **Example:** Keep your mouth shut. **(Active)**
 
 
 
 

 You are ordered to keep your mouth shut. **(Passive)**

• The following structure should be followed: **Let + object + be + V3**
 
• **Example:** Spread the clothes. **(Active)**
 
 

 Let the clothes be spread. **(Passive)**

 
• If the sentence gives a **moral suggestion(and has an object)**,** 'should'** is used as a **helping verb**.

 
 
• **Example:** Help the poor. **(Active)**
 
 

 The poor should be helped. **(Passive)**

 
• The given sentence gives a **moral suggestion(to avoid taking medicines without the doctor's prescription) and has an object i.e. medicine**, therefore,** 'should'** has been used.

 

**So, the final sentence is - ***Medicines should not be taken without the doctor's prescription.*

questions.question: P, Q and R can complete a task in 20, 30 and 60 days, respectively. How many days will it take to finish the work if P is helped by Q and R every third day?
questions.solution:
**Given:**

P can complete a task in 20 days,

Q in 30 days,

R in 60 days,

P is helped by Q and R every third day.

**Concept: **

Work done is reciprocal of the time taken. Use the concept of man-days.

**Solution:**

Total work = LCM(20, 30, 60) = 60 units

Efficiency of P = 60/20 = 3

Efficiency of Q = 60/30 = 2

Efficiency of R = 60/60 = 1

Work done by P in two days = 2 days × 3 = 6 units.

On third day, all three work together, their combined work = 3 + 2 + 1 = 6 units.

Therefore, in every cycle of three days, work done = 6 + 6 = 12 units.

To finish 60 unit of work, days required = 3 × 5 = 15 days.

**Hence, it will take 15 days to finish the work.**

questions.question: Ravi's salary was increased by 50%. After some time, his new salary was also increased by 50%. Find his gain percentage on the salary.
questions.solution:
[IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/ca81259519cadfb2d5350673c220e419e60378e9770ad26512fc8e826a8d93f1.png] __Shortcut Trick__

When a value is successively increased by x% and y%, the net percentage change is calculated using the successive percentage formula:

Net % Change = x + y + (x × y) ÷ 100

Here, both increments are 50% (so x = 50, y = 50).

Net % Change = 50 + 50 + (50 × 50) ÷ 100 = 100 + 25 = 125%

**∴ The correct answer is 125%.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/c76c13ba2d2ab46b47f8a931ae621dac081a0cb266b142dc23f58659fac4a466.png] **__Alternate Method__**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/959a3df6cdaa68bd3d15e0bd7156fc35e2b19dab12d7d01b98f3dc4b4278de3d.png] 

**Given:**

First salary increase = 50%

Second salary increase = 50%

**Formula Used:**

Gain Percentage = (Total Gain ÷ Initial Salary) × 100%

**Calculations:**

⇒ Let the initial salary of Ravi be 100 units.

⇒ After the first 50% increase, salary = 100 + (50% of 100) = 150 units.

⇒ After the second 50% increase, salary = 150 + (50% of 150) = 150 + 75 = 225 units.

⇒ Total Gain = Final Salary − Initial Salary = 225 − 100 = 125 units.

⇒ Gain Percentage = (125 ÷ 100) × 100% = 125%.

**∴ The correct answer is 125%.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__**

Successive Percentage Formula

When a value undergoes two successive percentage changes of a% and b%, the effective percentage change is [a + b + (a × b) ÷ 100]%. Remember to use a negative sign if it involves a decrease.

Multiplier Method (Fractional Equivalent)

A 50% increase means the new value becomes 150% (or 3/2) of the original base. Two successive 50% increases mean multiplying the base by (3/2) × (3/2) = 9/4. This represents an overall increase of 5/4 over the initial value, which is exactly 125%.

Base Change Implication

A common exam mistake is simply adding the percentages directly (50% + 50% = 100%). However, successive calculations must factor in that the second percentage increase operates on an already enlarged base, which intrinsically leads to a higher net gain.
</p

questions.question: If the population of a town increases by 40% in the first year and decreases by 30% in the second year, find the net percentage change.
questions.solution:

Population increases by 40% in the first year.

Population decreases by 30% in the second year.

**Formula Used:**

Net Percentage Change = (a + b + (ab)/(100)) 

**Calculation:**

Let the initial population be 100.

After a 40% increase in the first year:

Population = 100 + 40 = 140

After a 30% decrease in the second year:

Population = 140 - 0.3 × 140

Population = 140 - 42

Population = 98

Net Percentage Change:

Initial population = 100

Final population = 98

Change in population = 98 - 100 = -2

Net Percentage Change = (-2)/(100) times 100

Net Percentage Change = -2%

**The net percentage change in the population is a decrease of 2%.**

__
 
• The power of the Governor to promulgate ordinances during the recess of the legislature in India is mentioned in **Article 213 of the Indian Constitution.**
 
• **Article 213** empowers the Governor of a state to promulgate ordinances when the legislative assembly or either house of the legislature (in the case of a bicameral legislature) is not in session.
 
• These ordinances have the same force and effect as an act of the state legislature but are temporary in nature and must be approved by the legislature within a** certain period.**

**​** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Constitutions typically consist of multiple articles that outline the fundamental principles, structures, and functions of a country's government.** While the specific articles and their content can vary from one constitution to another, I can provide you with a general overview of common articles found in many constitutions:
 
• **Preamble: **This sets out the purpose, values, and aspirations of the constitution.
 
• **Fundamental Rights and Freedoms:** These articles outline the individual rights and freedoms that citizens are entitled to, such as freedom of speech, religion, and assembly, as well as rights related to equality, privacy, and due process.
 
• **Structure of Government:** These articles describe the structure of the government, including the separation of powers between the legislative, executive, and judicial branches. They may also define the roles and responsibilities of each branch and the system of checks and balances.
 
• **Head of State and Government: T**hese articles outline the powers, duties, and limitations of the head of state and government, which may include a president, monarch, or prime minister.
 
• **Legislature: **These articles establish the composition, powers, and functions of the legislative body, such as the parliament or congress. They may detail the process of lawmaking, representation, and electoral systems.
 
• **Executive: **These articles define the powers, responsibilities, and selection process of the executive branch, which may include the president, prime minister, or a council of ministers. They often outline the executive's authority to implement laws and administer the government.
 
• **Judiciary:** These articles establish the structure and jurisdiction of the judicial system, including the courts and their powers. They may outline the appointment and tenure of judges, as well as the principles of judicial independence and the right to a fair trial.
 
• **Constitutional Amendments**: These articles specify the procedures and requirements for amending the constitution itself, ensuring that any changes are made through a formal and transparent process.
 
• **Territorial Organization:** These articles define the territorial boundaries, administrative divisions, and relations between the central government and local or regional authorities.
 
• **Transitional Provisions: **In some constitutions, there may be specific articles that address the transition from a previous constitutional order, such as after a regime change or a significant political event.

__
 
• According to Article 169 of the Constitution of India, the Parliament of India can create or abolish the State Legislative Council of a state by a simple majority if that state's legislature passes a resolution for that with a special majority. 
 
• The State Legislative Council can neither form nor dissolve a state government.
 
• The State Legislative Council also have no role in the passing of money bills. 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

• Legislative Council (Vidhan Parishad):

 
 
• Legislative Council is the upper house of the state. 
 
• A member of a legislative council is referred to as an MLC.
 
• The Constitution of India does not mandate states to form a Legislative Council.
 
 
 
• What is the difference between the Legislative Assembly and the Legislative Council?
 
 
• The term of the Legislative Assembly is five years unless it is dissolved earlier at the request of the chief minister. The tenure of the members of the council is six years and a third of the members of the House retire after every two years.
 
• The Legislative Assembly is the lower house, much like the Lok Sabha of the Parliament. Legislative Council is the upper house in the state and like the Rajya Sabha, it is a permanent House.
 
 
 
• How is the Legislative Council created?
 
 
• The members of the Council are either nominated by the Governor of the state or are indirectly elected.
 
 
• One-third of the members of this House are elected by the Legislative Assembly.
 
• One-third are elected by the local bodies like a municipality or other local authorities.
 
• One-twelfth of the members are elected by graduates.
 
• One-twelfth of the members are elected by teachers.
 
• One-sixth of the members are nominated by the Governor.
 
 
 
• The legislative Council elects its Chairman, who plays the role of presiding officer and Deputy Chairman from amongst its members.

questions.question:
With reference to the joint sitting of Parliament, which statement/s is/are correct?

(1) Article 109 provides for the joint sitting of both Houses in certain cases.

(2) The Lok Sabha Speaker presides the joint sitting of the two Houses of Parliament. 

Select the correct answer using the code given below -
questions.solution:
The correct answer is **Only 2.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

**Joint sitting of Parliament** 

 
• **Constitutional Provision: Article 108 **of the Indian Constitution provides for a joint sitting of both Houses of Parliament. It states that if a bill has been passed by one House and rejected by the other, or if amendments made by one House have not been accepted by the other, then **the President of India** may summon a joint sitting for the purpose of resolving the deadlock. ***Hence, Statement 1 is not correct.***
 
• **Presiding Officer: **The** Speaker of the Lok Sabha presides over the joint sitting.** If the Speaker is unavailable, the Deputy Speaker or any other member of the Lok Sabha chosen by the President presides. ***Hence, Statement 2 is correct.***
 
• **Quorum and Voting: **The quorum for a joint sitting is** one-tenth of the total number of members of both Houses.** In case of a vote, the decision is taken by a simple majority of the members present and voting. The presiding officer does not have a casting vote in case of a tie.
 
• **Conducting Business:** During a joint sitting, the Speaker announces the purpose of the sitting and then proceeds with the business on the agenda, which usually includes the consideration and voting on the bill or bills that led to the summoning of the joint sitting.
 
• **Powers and Limitations: **The joint sitting has the authority to pass the bill by a simple majority, irrespective of the decision of either House. However, it cannot amend the Constitution or introduce new legislation. It can only consider and vote on the bill or bills that led to the deadlock between the two Houses.
 
• **Occurrence:** Joint sittings of Parliament in India are relatively rare. They have occurred on a few occasions in the past to resolve differences between the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha on specific bills.
 
• For example, a joint sitting was held in 2002 to pass the Prevention of Terrorism Act, and in 1978 to pass the Banking Services Commission (Repeal) Bill.
